r: MKT 1260 teaches customer satisfaction development, loyalty building, rapport creation, and expectation management for consumer and business buyers, mapping to Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships and Communicating with Persons Outside Organization. Routine service interactions such as order status, basic troubleshooting, and scripted rapport-building are already within AI's competence: a productivity RCT measuring customer-support work found the largest gains accrued to novice agents using AI assistance, direct evidence this task category is exposed now. Yet Census BTOS diffusion data show only a minority of firms had deployed production AI by late 2025, so adoption lags capability and many service roles still route through human agents. No general-studies designation or accreditation mandate constrains this lower-level elective, and it is not a prerequisite for later coursework. The instrumental case is partially eroded for routine service tasks at this horizon, while complaint escalation and loyalty-building retain some near-term human necessity.

By 2031, AI-driven service agents should competently handle the large majority of the satisfaction, loyalty, and expectation-management tasks this course teaches, extending well beyond scripted interactions into personalized retention offers and proactive complaint resolution. Observed-usage data already place consumer- and business-facing service work among heavily used AI categories, and the productivity gains documented for support tasks compound as capability improves along the METR/Epoch trend of rapidly lengthening task-time horizons AI can complete unsupervised. With no embodiment barrier, no licensure or general-studies lock, and no foundational role feeding later courses, nothing structural caps the rating. The applied work of this course, diagnosing customer needs and responding appropriately, is performed competently by AI with limited human input in the modal case. The rating is High: the instrumental need for a student to acquire these specific service skills through coursework is substantially diminished by this horizon.

A decade out, service interactions across most channels should be AI-mediated by default, with human agents concentrated in exception-handling, high-value account management, and situations requiring genuine relational trust rather than routine satisfaction or loyalty tasks. The course's core content of rapport, expectation management, and loyalty mechanics describes exactly the terrain capability trends suggest AI will occupy most thoroughly, and no institutional or foundational constraint intervenes to protect it. The rating remains High, though ten-year forecasting carries real uncertainty: macro estimates of AI's economy-wide productivity effect over a decade remain modest, implying diffusion could still lag capability well into the 2030s, and some categories of relationship-dependent service work may prove more durable than a pure capability read implies. Confidence in the direction is stronger than confidence in the exact pace, but the instrumental case for this course is not one the evidence supports preserving.
MKT 1260.n: September 2026 evidence update. Task automatability (F1) raised at 24 months from 3 to 4. Introductory front-line customer service skills (building satisfaction and rapport, managing customer expectations) map directly onto scripted customer-service work. The Bureau of Labor Statistics' 2025-35 projections put customer service representatives at -5%, and Stanford's August 2026 payroll update and Anthropic's usage data both place customer service among the most automated occupations. The signal is descriptive, not causal. Rating changed (24 months: Medium to High); confidence lowered one step because the supporting labor data are descriptive. The original paragraph below is retained for transparency.
MKT 1260.d: This course introduces the field of customer service as applied to both consumer and business buyers. Areas covered include: developing customer satisfaction, building customer loyalty, creating rapport, and managing customer expectations. Students will identify these areas through class lectures, guest speakers, cases, and homework assignments. Students will also learn about career opportunities.

r: MKT 1985 places students in an approved workplace for hands-on professional experience, mapping to Getting Information, Communicating with Supervisors, Peers, or Subordinates, and Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships within a live organizational setting. The applied work is not a fixed task set AI performs but an in-person socialization process: learning workplace norms, professional conduct, and career navigation through direct human supervision. Task-exposure research consistently finds manual, physical, and real-time interpersonal categories least exposed, and an internship's value lies precisely in embodied presence within an employer's environment rather than in output AI could substitute. No general-studies designation applies, and the course carries no accreditation mandate, but the instrumental need here rests on presence rather than institutional lock. At this horizon, AI can support specific tasks a student performs during the internship, yet the course's own purpose, supervised professional experience, is untouched by that assistance.

By 2031, AI tools will likely handle more of the discrete tasks students encounter during an internship placement, from drafting documents to research support, but the course's instrumental function is professional socialization, not task completion. Employers still require candidates to demonstrate workplace judgment, collaboration, and professional conduct developed through direct interpersonal exposure, categories task-exposure research continues to classify as comparatively low-exposure relative to writing- or programming-heavy work. Diffusion data show adoption spreading unevenly across firms and industries, meaning many internship placements will still emphasize hands-on, supervised experience regardless of what AI can technically do elsewhere in the organization. No foundational or institutional lock protects this course, but none is needed: its value is inherently embodied. The rating holds Low, with the caveat that the specific tasks interns perform day-to-day will keep shifting as workplace AI use expands.

Ten years out, the workplace an intern enters will almost certainly be more AI-saturated, and the specific deliverables a business intern produces may look quite different from today's. But the course's instrumental purpose, supervised exposure to professional norms, career exploration, and interpersonal competence within a real organization, does not reduce to a task list AI can complete on a student's behalf. Embodied, real-time interpersonal work remains the category task-exposure research treats as most resistant to substitution, and nothing in the capability trend changes what it means to gain hands-on professional experience. Genuine uncertainty exists about whether internship structures evolve significantly by 2036, and about how thoroughly AI mediates the tasks interns are assigned, but the requirement for supervised, in-person professional experience is a durable feature of business education that this rating reflects with reasonable confidence.
MKT 1985.d: Approved internships introduce the specific field of business as well as provide an opportunity to gain practical, hands-on professional work experience. Students will learn about the profession, explore related career paths, and increase professionalism.

r: MKT 2010 applies global marketing strategy across price, product, distribution, and promotion in developed and developing markets, requiring cultural analysis and evaluation of market-entry modes, tasks mapping to Analyzing Data or Information and Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others. This content sits in a highly exposed category: marketing strategy work is among the categories task-exposure research and observed-usage data both associate with heavy AI use already. But the course carries a General Studies: Social and Behavioral Sciences, Global Diversity designation, a gtPathways-style transfer-core requirement that functions as an institutional lock regardless of the underlying task automatability. That designation caps the rating at Low for this horizon independent of how exposed the applied marketing content itself is. The binding constraint here is not embodiment or verification burden but curricular mandate: the course must remain available as a transfer-credit-bearing gen-ed option, which the instrumental-automation analysis does not override.

By 2031, AI should competently perform most of the analytical and content-generation work underlying global marketing strategy, including competitive scanning, cultural-context research, and positioning drafts across markets, placing the applied task set solidly in the automatable range task-exposure research assigns to marketing-adjacent work. Absent any institutional constraint, that would support a High rating. The gtPathways-style General Studies designation, however, caps the rating at Medium regardless of task exposure: the course must remain available to satisfy a statutory transfer-core requirement, and that mandate does not loosen based on AI capability. The rating therefore reflects a ceiling set by curricular structure rather than by diminished instrumental value of the marketing content itself. Confidence in the underlying exposure judgment is reasonably high; the institutional cap is the dominant and more durable factor shaping this rating at the five-year horizon.

A decade out, global marketing analysis, cultural-context research, and market-entry evaluation should be thoroughly within AI's competence, consistent with the capability trend of rapidly lengthening task-time horizons and continued diffusion of AI tools into competitive-intelligence and strategy work. Were this an unconstrained upper-division elective, that capability trajectory alone would likely support a High rating by 2036. But the course's General Studies: Social and Behavioral Sciences, Global Diversity designation is a structural transfer-core requirement unlikely to be eliminated within a decade purely because AI performs the underlying tasks well; gen-ed frameworks change on institutional and legislative timelines, not capability timelines. The rating holds at Medium, capped by that designation rather than by any residual task the analysis suggests AI cannot perform. Ten-year uncertainty is real, but it concerns capability specifics more than whether the institutional lock persists.
MKT 2010.d: Students study the importance of globalization in the business world where global markets are more connected and marketers must respond to the expectations of global consumers. The course covers the essential concepts of global marketing with the aid of extensive, real-life examples. The course offers balanced coverage of developed and developing markets. Integrating cultural analysis throughout the course, students examine global and local competition and forms of global market entry, as well as basic principles of global marketing strategies, such as price, product, distribution, and promotion.

r: MKT 2250 introduces the professional-selling environment from both consumer and business-buyer perspectives, covering sales-process stages and selling ethics, work mapping to Selling or Influencing Others and Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships. Substantial parts of the sales process, including prospect research, outreach drafting, and CRM-driven lead qualification, are already AI-assisted in practice, consistent with productivity research showing large task-speed gains from AI copilots on structured knowledge work. The core selling moments the course emphasizes, however, remain real-time interpersonal exchanges: building trust, reading buyer hesitation, closing under negotiation. That mixed profile, some tasks squarely automatable and others resistant, supports a Medium rating rather than High at this horizon. No general-studies designation or foundational role constrains the course independently; the rating reflects genuine partial exposure of the sales-process content itself rather than an institutional cap.

By 2031, AI should competently handle the great majority of the sales-process tasks this course introduces, including qualifying prospects, personalizing outreach, structuring proposals, and even simulating objection-handling for training, extending materially beyond today's copilot-assisted prospecting into more autonomous deal-support roles. Task-exposure research's finding that programming- and writing-adjacent tasks skew toward high exposure extends reasonably to the drafting and analytical components of professional selling, and no embodiment, licensure, or foundational barrier caps this elective. The residual, live persuasion and relationship trust in high-stakes negotiations, persists but represents a narrowing share of what the course actually teaches as sales moves toward AI-mediated channels. The rating moves to High: the instrumental case for learning the full sales process through this specific course is substantially eroded, even though closing skill in complex deals likely remains valuable longer.

Ten years out, AI-mediated selling, including automated outreach, dynamic pricing negotiation, and AI sales agents handling routine transactions end-to-end, should be commonplace, and the applied tasks underlying this introductory course largely automated. The rating remains High, consistent with the capability trend toward AI completing longer, more autonomous task sequences without direct human execution. Genuine uncertainty attaches to this horizon: the jagged frontier documented in current research shows AI users perform markedly worse outside AI's actual competence, so persuasion in high-stakes or novel negotiations may retain a durable human role that a pure capability projection understates. Diffusion could also lag well behind capability, as macro estimates of AI's economy-wide productivity effect over a decade remain modest. The direction is confidently High; the exact residual share of selling that stays human-led by 2036 is the genuinely uncertain part of this forecast.
MKT 2250.d: This course introduces the environment of professional selling and presents both consumers' and business buyers' perspectives. Areas covered include ethical considerations in professional selling and elements in the sales process. Students will meet industry representatives during classroom discussions to learn about potential career opportunities.

r: MKT 3000 covers the marketing process of analyzing, planning, implementing, and controlling programs to create, deliver, and communicate customer value, mapping to Developing Objectives and Strategies and Analyzing Data or Information. Marketing content generation, segmentation analysis, and campaign drafting rank among the most exposed activities in task-exposure research, and observed-usage data show writing- and office-adjacent work prominent in current AI use, so the instrumental case for execution-level marketing tasks is already partially eroded. Diffusion still lags capability, however, and the course's strategic framing, understanding buyer exchange, competitive positioning, and full marketing-mix logic, carries more residual value near-term than any single executional task. Only a weak AACSB accreditation credit floor applies here, not a course-specific mandate. The rating is Medium: real erosion for content-generation tasks, tempered by the strategic and integrative judgment the course still teaches at this horizon.

By 2031, AI should competently perform the large majority of marketing execution work, including content, copy, segmentation, campaign analysis, and increasingly personalization at scale, broadly automating the applied tasks to which this course's knowledge is put. Task-exposure research and observed-usage data both place marketing-content generation among the most exposed activity categories, and no embodiment, licensure, or foundational constraint intervenes; AACSB accreditation sets no course-specific mandate strong enough to cap the rating. The residual is brand strategy and integrative judgment across the marketing mix, real but a fraction of what an introductory principles course covers. The rating is High: the applied work this course prepares students to do is performed competently by AI with limited human input by this horizon, even as the strategic framing retains some standalone value.

A decade out, AI should perform nearly all marketing execution and a substantial share of strategic analysis too, given the capability trend toward longer, more autonomous task completion and continued diffusion into marketing-technology stacks. The instrumental case for a principles-of-marketing course shifts toward the oversight and high-level judgment roles held by a shrinking share of practitioners. The rating holds High, hedged by real ten-year uncertainty: macro productivity estimates over a decade remain modest, suggesting diffusion could still lag capability meaningfully, and brand or strategic judgment may sustain more human marketing work than a pure capability read implies. Among College of Business core courses, marketing content remains among the more exposed precisely because its applied output sits squarely in the highest-exposure categories task-exposure research identifies, even accounting for that uncertainty.
MKT 3000.d: This course helps students understand marketing, the process through which organizations analyze, plan, implement, and control programs to develop and maintain beneficial exchanges with target buyers. Effective marketing is critical for the long-term success of any business organization because this function ensures that the firm attracts, retains, and grows customers by creating, delivering, and communicating superior customer value.

r: MKT 3010 teaches systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of marketing data using qualitative and quantitative methods to generate actionable business insight, mapping directly to Analyzing Data or Information and Processing Information. This is squarely quantitative-analyst-type work, a category task-exposure research explicitly identifies among the most exposed occupations, and observed-usage data show Computer & Mathematical activity as the largest current AI-usage category by a wide margin. Survey design, statistical analysis, coding of qualitative data, and insight synthesis are already meaningfully AI-assisted in research practice. The work is fully digital, with no embodiment barrier, and no general-studies designation or foundational role constrains the course. Verification burden is moderate rather than minimal, since flawed research can mislead costly business decisions, but that alone does not clear the dampener threshold. The rating is High already at this horizon: the applied analytical tasks are both AI-competent and increasingly deployed in research practice.

By 2031, AI should handle the substantial majority of marketing research execution, including instrument design support, large-scale qualitative coding, statistical modeling, and synthesis into client-ready insight reports, consistent with the METR/Epoch trend of AI completing steadily longer analytical task sequences with less direct supervision. The course's core content maps closely onto the quantitative-analyst work task-exposure research flags as most exposed, and the fully digital nature of the work means no embodiment factor tempers that exposure. No accreditation or foundational constraint applies. The rating remains High: the instrumental need to acquire these specific research-execution skills through coursework is substantially diminished, even as human researchers retain a role framing the right questions and validating that automated analysis actually answers the business problem posed.

Ten years out, AI-driven research platforms should be capable of end-to-end marketing research, spanning design, fielding, analysis, and insight generation, with human involvement concentrated in defining research questions and validating high-stakes conclusions rather than executing the analytical pipeline this course teaches. The rating remains High, anchored in the same quantitative, fully digital task profile that places this content among the most exposed in task-exposure research. Ten-year forecasts carry inherent uncertainty, and macro estimates of AI's decade-long productivity effect remain comparatively modest, suggesting some organizations may still rely on human-executed research methods well into the 2030s due to trust, data-access, or procurement lags rather than capability limits. The direction of this rating is held with reasonable confidence given how squarely the course's content sits within AI's demonstrated analytical strengths.
MKT 3010.d: This course provides students with a systematic and objective approach to collecting, analyzing, and interpreting marketing data to generate actionable insights that support the identification of marketing problems and support informed decision- making. Students develop skills in both qualitative and quantitative research methods.

r: MKT 3100 teaches a strategic-planning approach to developing and managing the retail marketing mix, mapping to Developing Objectives and Strategies and Analyzing Data or Information as students plan pricing, assortment, and promotional tactics for a retail context. This strategic-planning work resembles the marketing-content and analysis categories task-exposure research classifies as highly exposed, and current AI use already touches retail analytics and merchandising planning support. Adoption remains uneven, though: Census BTOS diffusion data show only a minority of firms had production AI deployed by late 2025, and much retail-mix planning still involves judgment about local market conditions and competitive response that current tools support rather than replace outright. No general-studies designation or foundational role applies. The rating is Medium: meaningful exposure of the planning tasks the course teaches, tempered by diffusion lag and residual strategic judgment at this near-term horizon.

By 2031, AI should competently handle the large majority of retail marketing-mix planning, including dynamic pricing recommendations, assortment optimization, promotional calendar generation, and competitive scanning, extending well past today's decision-support tools into more autonomous planning roles. Task-exposure research's classification of marketing-adjacent strategic and analytical work as highly exposed applies directly here, and no embodiment, accreditation, or foundational constraint caps the rating. The residual is judgment calls unique to a given retail brand's positioning and local market nuance, real but a narrowing share of what strategic retail planning as taught in this course actually requires. The rating is High: the instrumental case for learning retail-mix planning through this specific coursework is substantially diminished by this horizon, even as brand-specific strategic framing retains some standalone value for practitioners.

A decade out, AI-driven retail planning platforms should handle pricing, assortment, and promotional strategy with limited human input across most retail contexts, consistent with the broader capability trend toward AI completing longer strategic-planning sequences autonomously. The rating remains High. Genuine ten-year uncertainty applies, however: macro estimates of AI's economy-wide productivity effect over a decade remain modest, and retail strategy tied to physical store formats, local competitive dynamics, and brand identity may retain more durable human involvement than a pure capability projection suggests. Diffusion into small and mid-size retail organizations, which still make up much of the sector, could also lag well behind what large retailers deploy. The direction of the rating is held with reasonable confidence, given how closely this course's strategic-planning content tracks the most-exposed marketing-analysis categories, even allowing for that residual uncertainty.
MKT 3100.d: This course will familiarize the student with fundamental retailing concepts and practices. Emphasis will be given to a strategic-planning approach for developing and managing the retail marketing mix.

r: MKT 3110 covers advertising and promotional strategy and tactics, environmental scanning, creative-strategy development, and planning messages across multiple promotional platforms, mapping to Thinking Creatively and Developing Objectives and Strategies. Advertising copy and content generation are among the specific activities task-exposure research and observed-usage data both identify as most exposed to AI, and a professional-writing productivity RCT found AI assistance cut task time by roughly forty percent while raising quality, direct evidence this exact category of work is already competently AI-performed. Campaign platform planning, message drafting, and creative-concept generation are fully digital tasks with no embodiment barrier. No general-studies designation or foundational role constrains this elective. The rating is High already at this horizon: the course's core applied content, generating and managing advertising and promotional messaging, sits precisely in the category the evidence shows is most exposed and most actively deployed.

By 2031, AI should handle the substantial majority of advertising and promotion execution, including copy generation, creative variant testing, multi-platform campaign planning, and performance-driven optimization, extending the productivity gains already documented in professional writing tasks into fuller campaign-management autonomy. The course's content maps directly onto the highest-exposure categories task-exposure research identifies, and the fully digital, non-embodied nature of the work means no protective factor tempers that exposure at this horizon. No accreditation or foundational constraint applies, and diffusion by this point should be far more advanced than today's uneven adoption. The rating remains High: the instrumental need to learn advertising execution through this specific coursework is substantially diminished, with the residual concentrated in overarching creative-brand judgment and cross-platform strategic coherence that increasingly sits alongside, rather than instead of, AI-generated creative work.

Ten years out, AI should generate and optimize the large majority of advertising and promotional content across platforms with limited direct human execution, consistent with the capability trend toward longer, more autonomous creative and analytical task completion. The rating remains High. Some hedge is warranted: macro estimates of AI's economy-wide productivity effect over a decade remain comparatively modest, and brand-defining creative direction, the strategic judgment about what a campaign should say and why, may retain a more durable human role than execution-level copy and platform planning. Diffusion across smaller agencies and in-house teams could also lag well behind large-agency adoption. The direction of the rating is held with strong confidence given how squarely this course's content sits within documented high-exposure, high-productivity-gain categories, even with that residual uncertainty about creative-direction judgment.
MKT 3110.d: This course provides an in-depth understanding and analysis of advertising and promotional strategies and tactics necessary in the management of all marketing communications. Students will engage in environmental scanning, develop a creative strategy, and plan for communicating a message across multiple promotional platforms.

r: MKT 3160 examines managing sales forces, the impact of leadership styles on individual and group performance, and habits associated with managerial and leadership success, mapping to Guiding, Directing, and Motivating Subordinates and Coaching and Developing Others. This is people-management and leadership-judgment work, a category task-exposure research associates with lower exposure given its reliance on critical-thinking and interpersonal skills, activities the same research finds negatively associated with AI exposure relative to writing- or programming-heavy tasks. AI can support sales-performance dashboards and coaching-script generation, but motivating a team, resolving interpersonal conflict, and exercising managerial judgment about people remain squarely human functions at this horizon. No general-studies designation or foundational role applies. The rating is Low: the course's core content is leadership judgment applied to people, a task category current evidence does not show AI competently performing or organizations meaningfully deploying it for.

By 2031, AI-assisted coaching tools, sales-performance analytics, and team-dynamics dashboards should meaningfully augment how sales leaders make decisions, giving managers better information for coaching and performance conversations even as the core leadership act, motivating a team, navigating interpersonal conflict, exercising judgment about people, remains human-executed. The jagged-frontier finding that AI users perform markedly worse outside the model's actual competence is relevant here: leadership judgment in ambiguous interpersonal situations sits outside AI's demonstrated strengths, and mis-calibrated trust in AI-generated management advice carries real risk. That shift from purely low-exposure toward augmented-but-human-led leadership work supports moving the rating to Medium. No institutional or foundational constraint caps it further. The instrumental case for learning sales leadership through this course is only partially eroded, concentrated in the analytical-support tasks around leadership rather than leadership itself.

A decade out, AI should be deeply embedded in sales-management analytics, coaching support, and performance forecasting, but the leadership functions this course centers, motivating people, building team culture, exercising judgment in ambiguous interpersonal situations, remain activities task-exposure research continues to associate with lower exposure due to their critical-thinking and interpersonal character. The rating holds at Medium rather than rising further, reflecting genuine but partial erosion concentrated in the analytical and administrative periphery of sales management rather than its interpersonal core. Ten-year uncertainty cuts both ways: capability could advance enough that even coaching and motivation become meaningfully AI-mediated, or leadership work could prove among the more durable categories in the entire curriculum. Given that ambiguity, Medium reflects real but bounded erosion rather than a confident projection toward High.
MKT 3160.d: In this course, students analyze the opportunities and challenges associated with managing effective sales forces. Various leadership styles and their respective impact on individual and group performance are also examined. Additionally, students have the opportunity to adopt personal habits that have, historically, enabled marketplace success and led to managerial and leadership positions.

r: MKT 3190 applies segmentation, positioning, branding, and marketing-mix concepts to social and behavioral-change objectives in nonprofit and for-profit contexts, including cause-related marketing and donor-relationship development, mapping to Developing Objectives and Strategies and Communicating with Persons Outside Organization. The underlying marketing-execution tasks resemble the highly exposed categories task-exposure research identifies elsewhere in the discipline, but messaging around health, environment, and social causes carries a materially higher verification burden than routine commercial marketing: missteps in socially sensitive messaging produce non-obvious, reputationally costly failures that require a knowledgeable human to catch before publication. That elevated verification burden drops the rating one band at this horizon. No general-studies designation or foundational role applies. The rating is Low: real task exposure in the underlying marketing mechanics, offset by the elevated oversight this socially sensitive application domain demands.

By 2031, AI should competently draft and optimize much of the campaign content, segmentation analysis, and donor-communication material this course addresses, consistent with marketing content generation's status as one of the most exposed activity categories in task-exposure research. But cause-related and social-impact messaging remains an application area where the jagged-frontier finding is especially salient: AI performs markedly worse outside its demonstrated competence, and cultural or social missteps in this domain are the kind of non-obvious failure that mis-calibrated trust makes more likely, not less, as automation increases. That sustained elevated verification burden keeps the rating one band below where raw task exposure alone would place it. No institutional or foundational constraint applies. The rating is Medium: substantial underlying automatability tempered by a verification burden specific to socially sensitive marketing contexts.

Ten years out, the marketing-execution tasks underlying cause-related and social-impact campaigns, including content generation, segmentation, and donor-communication drafting, should be thoroughly within AI's competence, consistent with the broader capability trend toward longer, more autonomous task completion across marketing disciplines. But the elevated verification burden inherent to socially sensitive messaging is not primarily a capability-gap problem that resolves simply because models improve; reputational and ethical stakes around health, environment, and social-cause communication continue to warrant a knowledgeable human review step regardless of horizon. The rating holds at Medium rather than rising to High, reflecting a durable dampener rather than residual task difficulty. Genuine ten-year uncertainty remains about how thoroughly organizations trust AI-generated social-cause messaging even once capability supports it, which is itself part of why the verification-burden cap is treated as persistent here.
MKT 3190.d: In this class, students will gain an in-depth understanding of how marketing principles can be applied to create short-term and lasting social change in both non-profit and for-profit organizations. Using case studies and projects, students will apply marketing concepts such as segmentation, positioning, branding, and the marketing mix in order to address behavior objectives. Along the way, students will explore global issues, including those relating to health, environment, that impact society, government entities, NGO's, and the community at large. Further topics include developing long- term relationships with donors, cause-related marketing, and the role of socially responsible and environmentally sustainable marketing strategies in for-profit organizations.

r: MKT 3200 covers the digital marketing stack: platform selection, content and campaign execution, measurement, and integrating digital tactics into overall strategy, plus explicit attention to legal and ethical implications. Observed-usage data identifies Computer & Mathematical work and writing or office tasks as the largest generative-AI usage categories, and campaign copy, ad creative, and reporting dashboards already draw heavily on these tools, mapping cleanly onto interacting-with-computers and documenting-information activities. No general-studies designation or accreditation clause binds this course beyond a weak AACSB umbrella. The rating holds at Medium rather than higher because diffusion still lags capability: Census BTOS survey data puts only a minority of firms running AI in production, and the course's own legal and ethical framing signals judgment that still needs a person who understands the underlying platform mechanics.

By 2031, the platform-operations core of this course — building campaigns, drafting content, running measurement dashboards, and translating results into actionable insight — should be broadly automatable. Task-exposure research classifies writing and programmatic tasks as strongly positively associated with exposure, and productivity studies on professional writing already show large time reductions alongside quality gains when AI assists drafting and editing, a pattern that generalizes to campaign copy and reporting. Nothing in the course's institutional profile — no general-studies lock, no licensure or accreditation floor — resists that trajectory. The residual is strategic integration: aligning digital tactics with overall business strategy and exercising the ethical judgment the course foregrounds. That residue is real but narrower than the tool-operation content the course spends most of its time teaching, so the rating moves to High.

A decade out, the platform and measurement work this course teaches is plausibly executed end-to-end by AI systems with limited human input, consistent with the capability-trend evidence showing task-time horizons for AI systems doubling every few months on a fast trajectory. The instrumental case for taking a course centered on digital-channel mechanics is substantially eroded under that central-case projection. The hedge is real: macro-level productivity evidence suggests aggregate diffusion effects have historically been modest and slow even when capability is available, and the legal and ethical judgment layer the course foregrounds could prove stickier than a pure capability read implies. The rating stays High, reflecting where the tool-execution content points, while acknowledging genuine uncertainty about how much strategic and compliance judgment remains distinctly human at that horizon.
MKT 3200.d: This course introduces students to the basics of digital marketing, including the process, platforms, and technologies used to build long-term customer relationships. The integration of digital marketing into the organization's overall marketing strategy is explored. The course emphasizes the legal and ethical implications of the field as well as the importance of planning, measurement, and actionable insights.

r: Professional Selling teaches the sales process itself — reading diverse customers, applying ethical and legal considerations, and working case studies of real selling situations. The applied work maps to selling-or-influencing and interpersonal-relationship activities, categories that task-exposure research treats as less directly exposed than writing or programming-adjacent tasks. AI sales-assist tools already draft outreach and summarize calls, which is real but partial support rather than substitution for the persuasion and rapport-building the course centers on. No general-studies or accreditation clause constrains the course; the operative brake is the jagged-frontier finding that AI performance degrades outside well-defined tasks, and live persuasion with a skeptical human counterpart sits closer to that edge. The rating holds at Medium, reflecting meaningful augmentation without the applied core being performed competently by AI end-to-end.

By 2031, AI will likely handle more of the preparatory and follow-up work around selling — prospect research, personalized messaging drafts, objection-handling rehearsal — while the live, adversarial negotiation moment retains its human center. Productivity research on customer-facing work shows the largest AI-driven gains accruing to novice performers on structured interactions, which is suggestive for coached selling scenarios but does not establish that AI closes deals unsupervised. The course's ethical and legal content also implies a verification layer for claims made to customers, a nontrivial constraint on autonomous AI selling given documented mis-calibrated trust when AI models operate outside their competence frontier. With no institutional lock pushing the rating down further, Medium is retained: meaningfully more augmented selling work, but the applied task the course teaches is not yet competently performed by AI without a person driving it.

Ten years out, conversational AI agents capable of live, adaptive persuasion across text, voice, and video channels are a plausible central-case development given the pace of capability growth documented in time-horizon trend data, and organizations adopting such agents would erode the instrumental need for training human sellers on the full case-based sales process this course teaches. The rating moves to High under that projection, while carrying real uncertainty: interpersonal trust-building with high-value or skeptical buyers has historically resisted full automation longer than content-generation tasks, and adoption of autonomous selling agents also depends on buyer acceptance, not just seller-side capability. The hedge is genuine — this could remain Medium if buyer-side resistance to AI-led selling persists — but the central capability trajectory points toward broad erosion of the course's applied relevance by 2036.
MKT 3250.d: Students will examine the environment of professional selling and the sales process. Areas covered include communicating with diverse customers, ethical and legal considerations in personal selling, and the elements of the sales process. This course has a case orientation.

r: Marketing of Services addresses service strategy, complaint management, service guarantees, and the interpersonal 'moment of truth' between employee and customer, alongside employee empowerment and measuring quality through relationship marketing. Much of the applied work — resolving conflicts, coaching frontline staff, performing in front of the public — sits in interpersonal categories that task-exposure research treats as less exposed than writing or data tasks. Productivity research on customer support does show meaningful AI-driven gains, concentrated among novice agents handling routine interactions, which supports partial automation of complaint triage and satisfaction measurement rather than the relationship-management core. No general-studies or accreditation lock applies. The rating holds at Medium: analytical measurement pieces (satisfaction scores, return-on-quality) are increasingly AI-assisted, but the employee-empowerment and moment-of-truth content resists full delegation at this horizon.

By 2031, AI-assisted complaint routing, sentiment analysis, and satisfaction measurement should be standard in service organizations, consistent with observed-usage data showing office and analytical tasks as heavily AI-touched categories already. That automates a meaningful share of the course's measurement content. The employee-empowerment and relationship-marketing material, however, describes managing human employees who manage human customers in real time — a chain of interpersonal work the jagged-frontier evidence suggests AI handles less reliably than bounded analytical tasks, with mis-calibrated trust a real risk if it is deployed there anyway. No institutional lock caps the rating. Given the balance — automated measurement layered on a still-human relationship core — Medium is retained rather than moving to High, reflecting that the applied tasks are only partially, not competently and broadly, performed by AI at this horizon.

A decade out, if AI-mediated service interactions (chat-based support, sentiment-driven service recovery, automated guarantee administration) become the default channel through which the 'moment of truth' occurs, then the human-employee-empowerment framing this course teaches becomes less instrumentally necessary — the moment of truth increasingly happens between a customer and a system rather than a coached employee. The rating moves to High under that central-case read of capability trends showing rapid growth in dialogue competence. The hedge is substantial: complaint resolution and service recovery for consequential purchases plausibly retain human oversight longer than routine service, and the course's real-life-example, case-based pedagogy could remain relevant to designing and supervising those human-AI service systems even if it does not remain relevant to executing them directly.
MKT 3300.d: This course will introduce students to the problems and issues that are unique to marketing a service organization as well as marketing services. Topics include service strategy, listening to customers, complaint management, service guarantees, customer satisfaction, measuring return on quality, managing moment of truth, relationship marketing, and employee empowerment.

r: Consumer Behavior teaches the theories and variables underlying purchase decision-making and their strategy implications — fundamentally an analytical, pattern-recognition discipline applied to human data rather than a hands-on or interpersonal one. Observed-usage data shows Computer & Mathematical work as the largest generative-AI usage category, and task-exposure research places quantitative-analyst-adjacent work among the most exposed occupations, both of which map onto the analyzing-data and processing-information activities this course builds toward. AI tools already generate consumer segments, predict purchase propensity, and summarize behavioral research literature competently. No general-studies designation or accreditation clause constrains the course. The rating sits at Medium at this horizon because applying behavioral theory to novel strategic situations — the course's stated learning target — still exceeds what deployed tools reliably do without expert framing.

By 2031, AI systems should competently perform the great majority of consumer-behavior analysis work: segmenting audiences, modeling purchase-decision variables, and translating patterns into strategy recommendations. GDPval-style evaluation of real deliverable quality shows leading models already approaching, though not yet matching, human expert output on this kind of analytical work, and the gap is on a fast-closing trajectory given documented capability growth. Nothing about this course's institutional standing — no gen-ed lock, no licensure clause — resists that trend. The theoretical grounding the course teaches becomes something AI applies directly to data rather than something a graduate must apply by hand. The rating moves to High: the instrumental case for a human performing this analysis, rather than directing and checking an AI system that performs it, is substantially weakened.

Ten years out, under the central capability trajectory implied by rapid task-time-horizon growth, consumer-behavior analysis — segmentation, predictive modeling of decision variables, strategy translation — is plausibly executed by AI with minimal human involvement in most commercial contexts. The rating remains High. The hedge concerns emerging or culturally novel consumer contexts where training data and pattern-matching are thinner; behavioral prediction in genuinely new categories may still benefit from a person who understands the underlying theory rather than trusting an automated pattern-match, especially given evidence that AI users show reduced accuracy and miscalibrated trust once they operate outside a model's competence frontier. That residual is real but narrow relative to the course's broad analytical content, so the ten-year rating holds High with appropriately wide uncertainty bands rather than a confident point estimate.
MKT 3310.d: This course analyzes the underlying theories and complex variables influencing consumers and their purchase decision-making processes. The marketing strategy implications of consumer behavior concepts are studied.

r: Inside Sales explicitly frames itself around a domain already reshaped by technology and automation — remote, screen-mediated selling built on CRM tools, virtual meetings, and streamlined process. That framing maps closely onto interacting-with-computers alongside selling-or-influencing activities, and generative AI already drafts outreach sequences, personalizes email cadences, and summarizes call recordings, functions that speed measurably documented in coding and writing productivity research plausibly extend to sales-enablement workflows. No general-studies designation or accreditation clause applies. The rating sits at Medium rather than High at this horizon because the live, real-time persuasion moment on a call or video meeting remains a distinctly human skill the course teaches directly, and firm-level AI adoption data shows deployment still concentrated in a minority of organizations, keeping realized automation behind raw capability.

By 2031, AI sales-development agents handling prospecting, sequencing, and much live-chat qualification should be common, consistent with observed-usage evidence showing automation (rather than augmentation) as the dominant usage pattern in enterprise contexts already. Because inside sales is virtual and screen-mediated by design — the course's own premise — it sits closer to AI's digital comfort zone than field or relationship-based selling. The remaining human role is closing complex or high-value deals and handling escalated objections, a narrower slice of the course's content than the streamlined-process material it emphasizes. No institutional lock applies. The rating moves to High: the applied virtual-selling tasks the course trains toward are substantially performed by AI systems with limited human input at this horizon, even though full autonomy is not assumed.

A decade out, given the trajectory of AI capability growth in dialogue and negotiation and the fact that inside sales was already trending toward automation at the time this course was written, it is plausible that most remote, virtual-channel selling is AI-mediated by default, with humans concentrated in oversight, exception-handling, and the highest-value accounts. The rating holds High. The hedge is that buyer-side trust in AI-led sales interactions, not just seller-side capability, gates real-world deployment, and organizational and cultural resistance to fully automating a revenue-generating human relationship could slow this more than a pure capability read suggests. Genuine ten-year uncertainty remains, but the course's own premise — that inside sales already leans on technology and automation — points toward continued, not reversed, erosion of its instrumental necessity.
MKT 3320.d: Inside sales and remote sales are a growing proportion of bottom-line sales results. Such an expansion is motivated by an increased reliance on technology and automation, changing buyer attitudes towards salespeople, and the desire for a more streamlined process. This course focuses on the skills and competencies that are critical for today's demanding virtual selling environment.

r: Marketing and Sales Metrics is explicitly a data-driven-techniques course: segmentation, pricing, prospecting, customer valuation, campaign optimization, and ROI evaluation, mapping directly onto analyzing-data and evaluating-information-against-standards activities. Task-exposure research identifies quantitative-analyst-type work as among the most exposed occupational categories, and observed-usage data confirms Computer & Mathematical tasks as the largest generative-AI usage segment already in active deployment, not merely lab capability. AI dashboarding and analytics tools already compute segmentation models, pricing elasticity, and campaign ROI with limited expert intervention for well-specified problems. No general-studies designation or accreditation clause constrains the course, and it is not a prerequisite gating later required coursework. The rating is High even at this near-term horizon: the applied quantitative tasks the course teaches are already competently and increasingly commonly performed by AI tools in practice.

By 2031, the case for High strengthens further. GDPval-style evaluation of AI performance on real analytical deliverables shows leading models already approaching human-expert quality, and the pace of capability growth documented in time-horizon research suggests multi-step analytical workflows — building a segmentation model, running a pricing sensitivity analysis, assembling an ROI report — will be handled largely autonomously by AI systems within well-defined marketing-analytics workflows. No institutional lock offsets this. The residual human role narrows to framing the business question, validating unusual results, and making the final resource-allocation call, a smaller share of the course's tool-and-technique content than the analytical execution itself. The rating remains High, reflecting that the specific quantitative skills this course teaches are, for the most part, being performed by AI rather than merely assisted by it.

Ten years out, under the central capability trajectory, the quantitative marketing-analytics workflow this course teaches is plausibly executed end-to-end by AI systems with human involvement limited to oversight and strategic prioritization, not technique execution. The rating holds High. The hedge worth naming: aggregate productivity effects from AI diffusion have historically been modest even when raw capability is strong, so the pace at which organizations actually restructure analytics roles around AI-first workflows could lag the technical capability picture, and truly novel metrics problems without established templates may still draw on the applied statistical judgment the course builds. That said, among the ten courses in this batch, this one sits closest to the most-exposed end of the task-exposure literature, and nothing in its institutional profile pushes back against that reading.
MKT 3330.d: Marketing and sales have become increasingly reliant on data-driven techniques to solve business problems like segmentation, pricing, prospecting, customer valuation, campaign optimization, ROI, and more. This course focuses on tools and approaches to evaluate the impact of marketing and sales efforts.

r: Social Selling teaches online techniques for capturing buyer attention and positioning a seller as a helpful resource entirely through digital channels — content, profile positioning, and outreach conducted where buyers do due diligence, which is online. That is almost entirely a writing- and content-generation task mapped to interacting-with-computers and getting-information activities, and task-exposure research finds writing-heavy work strongly positively associated with AI exposure. AI tools already draft LinkedIn outreach, comment threads, and thought-leadership content competently, and observed-usage data shows office and writing tasks among the heaviest actual usage categories. No general-studies or accreditation lock applies. The rating is High even near-term: nearly the entire applied task set the course teaches — producing and distributing helpful-seeming online content to guide a buyer — is content generation of the kind AI already performs competently.

By 2031, AI-generated and AI-personalized social content, comment engagement, and prospect research should be standard practice for anyone attempting the course's core technique — becoming a visible, helpful digital presence to prospective buyers — since that entire workflow is text- and platform-native. Coding and writing productivity research showing large task-speed gains from AI assistance generalizes readily to this content-production loop, and no embodiment or licensure constraint offsets it. What remains human is deciding which relationships to prioritize and exercising judgment about authenticity in a channel increasingly saturated with AI-generated posts, a strategic layer distinct from the technique-execution content the course centers on. The rating stays High: the applied work of producing and distributing social-selling content is performed competently by AI with limited human input at this horizon.

A decade out, if online buyer research and social content consumption are themselves increasingly AI-mediated — buyers using AI assistants to evaluate vendors rather than reading individual posts — the entire premise of hand-crafted social-selling content aimed at a human reader is plausibly reshaped, not just automated but restructured, which this rating cannot fully anticipate. The rating holds High as the central-case read given the fast capability trajectory documented in time-horizon trend data, while carrying real ten-year uncertainty about whether the underlying channel (human social-media browsing) still functions the way the course assumes. That structural uncertainty, not a belief that the technique becomes harder to automate, is the main reason for hedging rather than treating High as a confident point estimate.
MKT 3350.d: Social Selling is a key resource for sales and marketing professionals seeking a better way to connect with today's customer where they're conducting due diligence - online. This course will show students how to capture the mindshare of business leadership and turn relationships into sales. Students will learn the online techniques used to be seen as a helpful resource that can guide the buyer toward their ideal solution. This course will provide essential guidance on selling to the modern buyer.

r: Marketing Channels covers designing, selecting, and managing distribution systems and intermediaries, including logistics and international distribution — work centered on coordinating real organizations (distributors, retailers, logistics partners) and making structural decisions under real-world contractual and operational constraints. That maps onto coordinating-work-of-others and decision-making activities that task-exposure research treats as less directly exposed than writing or quantitative-analysis work, since it depends on negotiated relationships and physical-world logistics rather than content production. AI tools can support channel analysis (mapping intermediary networks, modeling logistics costs) but the negotiation, partner selection, and contractual structuring at the course's core sit outside that support role. No general-studies designation applies. The rating is Low at this near-term horizon: the applied channel-design and partner-management tasks are not yet competently and broadly performed by AI.

By 2031, AI-assisted logistics optimization and channel-network analysis should be more embedded in supply-chain and distribution decisions, consistent with the direction of observed-usage growth in analytical work generally. But channel design also involves negotiating with real intermediary businesses and managing international distribution relationships subject to jurisdiction-specific legal and logistical constraints — work the jagged-frontier evidence suggests AI performs less reliably outside well-bounded problems, with real risk of miscalibrated confidence if deployed there regardless. No institutional lock applies, but none is needed to explain the residual: this is relationship- and negotiation-heavy work by nature. The rating moves to Medium, reflecting that the analytical layer (network modeling, cost optimization) becomes more AI-assisted while the structural decision-making and partner relationship core remains substantially human-led.

Ten years out, AI systems capable of more sophisticated logistics modeling and even some negotiation support are plausible under the documented capability growth trajectory, and channel analytics could become largely automated. The rating holds Medium rather than moving higher because macro-level evidence on AI's aggregate productivity effect suggests diffusion into structurally complex, negotiation-dependent business processes has historically been slow even when analytical capability exists, and international distribution decisions carry legal, tariff, and relationship risk that plausibly keeps a human decision-maker in the loop longer than in purely digital marketing functions. The hedge here runs in both directions: channel work could prove more resistant to automation than this rating assumes given its negotiated, cross-organizational nature, or capability growth in agentic negotiation could erode it faster than the Medium rating implies.
MKT 3410.d: This course is a comprehensive examination of the theories and practice of marketing channels. The course covers the essential concepts, principles, and strategies of marketing distribution systems with the aid of extensive real-life examples. The various forms of intermediaries are studied. Students examine the basic decision areas of designing, selecting, and managing marketing channels. Attention is also given to logistics and international distribution.

r: Sports Marketing applies general marketing principles to teams, athletes, and events, plus the reverse use of sports to market products through sponsorship and promotional licensing — largely content, deal-structuring, and campaign work conducted in offices rather than at the point of competition. That maps onto selling-or-influencing and creative-communication activities that observed-usage data already shows heavy AI engagement in, particularly sponsorship-proposal drafting, promotional content, and licensing-campaign copy. Productivity research on professional writing shows meaningful time savings with quality gains when AI assists drafting, a pattern directly applicable to sponsorship pitch decks and promotional materials. No general-studies designation applies. The rating sits at Medium near-term: sponsorship deal negotiation and live-event marketing retain a meaningful in-person, relationship-driven residue the jagged-frontier evidence suggests AI does not yet reliably substitute for.

By 2031, AI should competently handle the content-production side of sports marketing — promotional campaigns, licensing materials, sponsorship proposal drafts, fan-engagement copy — consistent with writing tasks' strong positive association with exposure in task-exposure research. Sponsorship-deal analytics (valuing exposure, projecting ROI for a licensing agreement) is also increasingly automatable, similar to marketing-metrics work generally. What remains most human is closing high-value sponsorship relationships and live-event execution, a narrower slice of the course's total content than the promotional and licensing material it spends most of its time on. No institutional lock applies. The rating moves to High: most of the applied marketing-execution work the course teaches is performed competently by AI, with the relationship-closing residue not large enough to hold the course at Medium.

A decade out, under the central capability trajectory, sports-marketing content production, sponsorship analytics, and licensing-campaign design are plausibly executed largely by AI, with humans concentrated in high-value deal-closing and live-event judgment calls. The rating holds High. The hedge: sports marketing retains a genuinely public-facing, event-driven, emotionally charged dimension — fan experience, athlete relationships, live promotional moments — that could sustain more human involvement than a pure content-exposure read implies, and ten-year uncertainty about how AI-generated promotional content interacts with fan trust and brand authenticity is real. Still, the bulk of what this course teaches is the same content-and-campaign machinery found in general marketing courses, so it tracks the more exposed end of the batch rather than the protected, embodied end.
MKT 3500.d: This course is a study of how the principles of marketing are applied in the sports industry. The course examines the marketing of sports, teams, athletes, etc., as well as the use of sports to market products (e.g., sponsorship and promotional licensing).

r: Business-to-Business Marketing covers marketing goods and services to businesses, institutions, resellers, and government — buying processes built on RFPs, multi-stakeholder committees, and longer, relationship-dependent sales cycles distinct from ordinary consumer marketing. The lead-generation, account research, and proposal-drafting components map onto analyzing-data and communicating-with-outside-organizations activities that AI content and research tools already support fairly competently, consistent with observed heavy usage of writing and analytical tasks generally across current deployments. But the multi-stakeholder negotiation and institutional buying-committee navigation at the course's core sit closer to the interpersonal-relationship activities task-exposure research treats as comparatively less exposed. No general-studies designation applies to this course. The rating is Medium near-term: proposal and account-research support is increasingly AI-assisted, but the applied stakeholder-management work the course centers on is not yet broadly performed by AI.

By 2031, AI should handle more of the analytical and content-production layer of B2B marketing — account-based marketing personalization, RFP-response drafting, lead scoring, and market research — extending the productivity gains already documented in customer-facing and writing-heavy work to B2B sales-enablement functions. The institutional buying process itself, however, still requires navigating organizational stakeholders, procurement rules, and multi-party negotiation, work the jagged-frontier evidence suggests remains outside AI's most reliable zone, with real risk of misplaced confidence if deployed unsupervised there. No institutional lock changes this picture. The rating holds at Medium: substantial augmentation of the marketing-execution layer, but the applied task of managing complex institutional buying relationships that the course teaches is not yet competently performed by AI without a person driving the relationship.

Ten years out, under the documented trajectory of capability growth in analytical and increasingly agentic tasks, it is plausible that AI systems handle a substantial share of B2B lead qualification, proposal generation, and even structured negotiation support, narrowing the course's applied relevance. The rating moves to High under that central-case projection. The hedge is meaningful: institutional buying decisions for large, consequential B2B purchases often involve risk-averse committees that may prefer human accountability for a sale regardless of AI capability, and macro-level diffusion evidence suggests organizational process change lags technical capability. Genuine ten-year uncertainty remains about how much of complex institutional selling AI comes to handle directly versus merely support, but the capability and content-exposure trend both point toward continued erosion rather than a durable Medium plateau.
MKT 3610.d: In this course, students will investigate the activities involved in marketing goods and services to businesses, institutions, resellers, and government, with primary emphasis on business-to- business marketing.

r: International Marketing has students compare economic, political, and cultural environments, map foreign legal and regulatory frameworks, and identify viable market-entry opportunities — tasks aligned with the Analyzing Data or Information and Developing Objectives and Strategies work activities. Much of this is desk research and synthesis performed at a computer, placing it inside AI's current reach, and observed-usage data confirms AI is already used heavily for research synthesis and drafting comparative country briefs. Yet the course's central skill is judging which cultural or political signal actually changes a market-entry decision for a specific firm, a critical-thinking task that task-exposure research finds negatively associated with automation exposure. Diffusion remains uneven across firms conducting this analysis. No general-studies or accreditation mandate protects the course, so the Medium rating reflects real but partial erosion: the research groundwork is exposed, the interpretive judgment considerably less so.

By 2031, AI tools will handle a larger share of the comparative research — regulatory scans, tariff and trade-barrier summaries, competitor benchmarking across regions — that this course currently teaches students to produce manually. The capability trend toward longer task-time horizons suggests multi-step country analyses that once required a team become plausible for a single AI-assisted analyst, and the productivity literature on professional writing shows large time savings on exactly this kind of synthesis-heavy report. Still, evaluating political risk and cultural fit for a specific product and market remains a critical-thinking judgment call task-exposure research treats as comparatively protected, and no licensure or gen-ed lock exists to slow adoption further. The course holds at Medium rather than rising to High because the applied task retains an interpretive core that AI assists rather than fully replaces, though the balance is visibly shifting toward automation.

Over a ten-year horizon the capability trajectory implied by the METR/Epoch doubling trend makes it plausible that AI systems competently execute most of the analytical work this course teaches — synthesizing political, economic, cultural, and legal signals into an entry recommendation — with only spot human review. Nothing in the course's structure protects it at that distance: there is no embodiment requirement, no licensure gate, and no foundational role feeding required downstream courses, so neither the F4 nor F5 cap applies. This is a longer-horizon, lower-confidence projection rather than a confident forecast; the jagged-frontier literature warns that AI users misjudge situations outside a model's actual competence, and cross-cultural business judgment is a plausible edge case for exactly that failure. Still, the deterministic combination of a strong F1 rise and no institutional or embodiment protection points to High rather than a continued Medium.
MKT 3710.d: The primary objective of this course is to introduce students to the complexities involved in the international marketing process. This course will sensitize students to the economic, political, and cultural differences among nations as they affect marketing; introduce students to the framework of organizations, laws, and business practices as they affect marketing; and develop a student's ability to identify and evaluate marketing opportunities in the international marketplace.

r: Ethnic Representations in Marketing has students critique how marginalized groups have been portrayed in marketing media, assess whether contemporary 'racial projects' in consumer markets produce meaningful change, and build campaign plans that authentically represent diverse audiences — tasks mapped to Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others and Thinking Creatively. This work is centrally critical and socially contextual judgment, the category task-exposure research finds most negatively associated with automation exposure, and the stakes of getting representation wrong are high: a generated campaign or analysis that misreads racial context can cause real reputational and social harm. That verification burden means any AI-assisted drafting still needs a human who holds this specific cultural and theoretical knowledge to catch errors the jagged-frontier literature shows AI users are prone to miss. No gen-ed or accreditation mandate applies; the Low rating instead comes entirely from the analytical and verification protections built into the course's core skill.

Nothing about the applied task changes qualitatively by 2031: assessing whether a marketing campaign's racial representation is authentic, non-tokenizing, and historically informed remains a contextual judgment call rather than a pattern AI reliably reproduces well, even as general content-generation tools grow more capable elsewhere in the marketing curriculum. Observed-usage data shows automation concentrated in routine writing and analysis tasks, not in adjudicating contested social meaning, and the course's explicit charge — to challenge existing power structures and stereotypes — runs against the kind of pattern-matching that drives current model competence. The high error cost of an AI-generated campaign or analysis that misjudges racial context keeps verification burden low, which is protective, across this horizon. Confidence here is moderate rather than high because social and cultural interpretation is an area where model capability could improve unevenly and unpredictably over time.

A ten-year projection is necessarily more uncertain, but the structural reason for protection — high verification burden on socially and historically contextual judgment — does not obviously erode with raw capability gains the way routine content generation does. The capability-trend literature describes faster task-time horizons for well-specified technical tasks; adjudicating authentic versus tokenizing representation across intersecting identity groups is comparatively ill-specified and contested, the kind of task where the jagged frontier is likely to persist longest. Task-exposure research's finding that critical-thinking skill is negatively associated with exposure supports holding the course at Low rather than projecting convergence toward Medium or High. This is a hedge, not a certainty: if future systems demonstrably internalize this specific critical framework well enough to require no expert check, the rating would need revision, but no current evidence in the approved palette supports that shift happening within this window.
MKT 3750.d: In this course, students examine key constructs and theories that allow them to critically explore how ethnically and racially marginalized groups in the U.S. have faced issues of racism and white supremacy, including inaccurate portrayal in marketing media in support of institutionalized systems of power, privilege, and oppression. Students learn to assess racial projects in consumer markets to determine when these offer meaningful changes to racial oppression. Lastly, students challenge existing power structures and stereotypes in the marketing industry by creating informed marketing plans that authentically, accurately, and positively reflect segments in their diversity.

r: This course covers direct mail, planned giving, workplace-giving campaigns, and major-gift solicitation, mapping to Communicating with Persons Outside the Organization and Selling or Influencing Others. The campaign-design and appeal-writing components — drafting direct-mail copy, planning workplace-giving pushes, structuring special-event promotion — sit squarely in the writing and office-task category that observed-usage data shows is already heavily used with generative tools, and professional-writing productivity research reports large time savings on this kind of drafting. Major-gift and individual solicitation, however, depend on cultivating a specific donor relationship over time, work that is only partly digital and still leans on interpersonal trust-building. That mixed profile — some tasks already substantially assisted, others more resistant — supports Medium at 24 months rather than a higher or lower band, with no accreditation or gen-ed lock in play here.

By 2031 the balance in this course tips further toward automatable execution: campaign copy, segmentation of donor lists, event-promotion planning, and even first-draft major-gift proposal language are plausible candidates for AI assistance approaching competent, low-oversight output, consistent with the productivity literature's finding of large speed gains on writing-heavy deliverables. Task-exposure research's classification of writing as strongly positively associated with automation exposure applies directly to the bulk of what this course teaches. The relationship-cultivation core of individual and major-gift solicitation is not itself embodied or licensure-protected — it is simply harder to automate today, not institutionally shielded — so nothing in the factor structure caps the course below High. The rating reflects that most of the course's applied skillset, not only its most routine slice, is projected to be substantially AI-assisted by this horizon.

Ten years out, the capability trend toward longer, more autonomous task-time horizons makes it plausible that AI handles the great majority of fundraising campaign design, donor segmentation, and appeal drafting this course teaches, with human fundraisers concentrated on the highest-value relationship moments rather than the broader curriculum content. No general-studies designation, licensure, or foundational role protects the course at this distance, so the deterministic rule places it at High alongside the 5-year rating. This is a longer-range projection and carries the standard hedge: nonprofit fundraising still depends on personal trust in ways that resist full automation, and adoption among smaller nonprofits — the diffusion literature notes uneven AI uptake across firms — may lag well behind large-organization capability. The rating describes where the applied task set is headed, not a certainty that every fundraising task fully converts to AI execution.
MKT 3820.d: Students examine the various strategies used by nonprofit organizations to raise funds for operating, program, and capital needs. Topics include direct mail, planned giving, individual solicitation, workplace giving, special events, and major gift campaigns.

r: New Product Development has students run idea generation, product design, prototyping, market testing, and financial feasibility analysis for a new-product project, mapping to Thinking Creatively and Analyzing Data or Information. The financial-analysis and market-testing-data components are computer-based and already benefit from AI assistance in the way productivity gains apply to structured analytical work, but idea generation, physical or functional prototyping, and iterative design refinement still depend heavily on hands-on creative and material judgment that current systems perform unevenly. Observed-usage data shows the largest concentration of AI usage in computer and mathematical tasks rather than open-ended creative ideation and physical prototyping. That split — analytical subtasks exposed, creative and prototyping subtasks not yet reliably so — keeps the course at Low for the near term, with no gen-ed or accreditation mandate altering the calculation either way.

By 2031, generative design tools and AI-assisted market-testing platforms are likely to handle a larger share of concept screening, financial modeling, and even early-stage design iteration than they do today, consistent with the capability trend toward longer, more complex task-time horizons documented in recent forecasting work. Idea generation increasingly benefits from AI as a brainstorming partner, and prototyping workflows that are digital, such as CAD-based or simulation-based work, become more automatable even where physical fabrication does not. The course's applied task set is therefore projected to shift from mostly protected to a genuine mix, supporting Medium rather than Low or High.
