No licensure or foundational role caps the projection; the rating reflects a real but partial rise in exposure across the product-development pipeline rather than a wholesale takeover of the creative process itself.

At a ten-year horizon, the compounding capability trend — faster task-time-horizon doubling alongside continued compute scaling — makes it plausible that AI competently performs most of the analytical and even much of the generative work in new-product development: market-testing design and interpretation, financial viability modeling, and computer-aided concept generation and iteration. Nothing in the course's structure protects it at this distance — no embodiment requirement locks it to physical prototyping alone, no accreditation credit-hour floor names this specific course, and it is not a prerequisite substrate for other required courses. This is a longer-range, lower-confidence projection; physical prototyping and hands-on material judgment could remain a meaningful residue the rating understates, and the jagged-frontier literature cautions that AI users are less accurate outside a system's true competence. Still, the deterministic factor combination points to High.
MKT 3910.d: This course introduces students to the issues related to developing new products. These issues include creativity and innovation, idea generation, product design, prototyping, market testing, financial analysis, and managing the process for productivity, efficiency, and success. Through classroom and experiential learning activities, students will learn the concepts and skills of new product development and complete a new product project.

r: MKT 3980 places students in a supervised, faculty-mentored marketing role at an employer, doing work new to the student and reflecting on approved learning objectives — an experiential format rather than a fixed task list, mapped loosely to Communicating with Supervisors, Peers, or Subordinates and Documenting/Recording Information. Whatever marketing execution tasks the placement involves, such as content support, campaign work, or market research, may individually be exposed to AI assistance, but the course's instrumental function is supervised professional practice and workplace relationship-building, which is not itself a task AI performs. Diffusion of AI tools across the small and mid-size employers that host these placements remains uneven. Because the applied work varies by placement and the supervisory, reflective structure is central rather than incidental, the course sits at Low near-term, with confidence appropriately lower given how generic the catalog description is.

By 2031, the specific marketing tasks assigned to interns — content drafting, campaign analytics, social-media execution — are likely to be substantially AI-assisted at the host organizations themselves, which could shrink the routine-task portion of what an intern actually does and shift placements toward oversight, review, and coordination work. Observed-usage data already shows generative tools concentrated in exactly this kind of office and writing work. The supervised, reflective structure of the internship format is not eliminated by that shift, but the instrumental case for the specific tasks performed weakens as employers automate more of the entry-level work interns traditionally handled. That supports a move to Medium. No general-studies or accreditation designation is present, and confidence remains moderate given how much the actual task set depends on employer and placement, which the catalog description does not specify.

At ten years, it is plausible that entry-level marketing execution tasks at host organizations are largely automated, changing the character of what an internship placement even offers a student — more oversight and coordination of AI-assisted output, less hands-on execution of the routine tasks interns historically performed. That shift does not clearly push the rating to High, however, because the course's core value is supervised professional exposure and reflection rather than a fixed task list that maps cleanly onto F1's automatability logic, and no institutional lock or foundational role applies either. This is a low-confidence, longer-range projection: internship content is set placement-by-placement and the catalog description gives no task specificity to anchor a sharper forecast. The rating holds at Medium as a hedge between continued relevance of supervised experience and a real narrowing of the tasks interns are actually asked to perform.
MKT 3980.d: Internships provide practical, hands-on experience in a professional field related to marketing. The internship must be based on work that is new to the student and supervised by a marketing professional. Internship placements must be approved through the internship credit approval process. Once enrolled, internship coursework is supervised by a faculty member. Students will complete academic work that encourages reflection regarding the approved learning objectives for the internship. Internship requirements vary by department. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

r: MKT 3981 places students in a supervised sales role at an employer — live prospecting, presenting, and closing under a sales professional's mentorship — mapping directly to Selling or Influencing Others and Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships. Live selling is real-time interpersonal work: reading a buyer's hesitation, adjusting tone and pitch in the moment, building trust across a sales cycle. Task-exposure research classifies manual, in-person, and real-time interpersonal work as comparatively low-exposure relative to writing and programming tasks, and that protection applies squarely here even though some sales-support tasks, such as CRM notes or follow-up emails, are more automatable. The embodied, presence-dependent core of live selling is the binding constraint, not any accreditation or gen-ed designation, and it keeps the course at Low near-term despite AI's growing role in sales-support tooling generally.

AI sales-assistance tools are likely to handle more lead scoring, follow-up drafting, and pipeline analytics by 2031, but the placement's core instrumental task — a student conducting a live sales conversation, reading a counterpart's reactions, and closing a deal — is not something a language model performs; it is something a person does, sometimes with AI support in the background. That real-time interpersonal, presence-dependent character is the same protective factor task-exposure research associates with low exposure for manual and in-person work, and it persists at this horizon because presence itself, not just the analytical content of selling, is what the applied task requires from the student. No institutional lock changes the picture either way. The rating stays at Low; confidence is limited by the fact that the catalog description does not specify which sales tasks any given placement actually assigns.

Ten years is long enough that AI-mediated sales interactions, such as chat- and voice-based agents handling some transactional selling, could plausibly displace a portion of the lowest-complexity live selling this internship exposes students to, which is reflected in the underlying F1 factor rising modestly across the horizon. But the deterministic rule applies the embodiment dampener at every horizon where real-time interpersonal presence remains the task's defining feature, and complex B2B or relationship-based selling — the kind a supervised professional-selling internship is built around — is a plausible holdout even as simpler transactional selling shifts elsewhere. This is a hedge rather than a confident forecast: capability trend data suggests fast general improvement, but the diffusion literature notes adoption lags capability unevenly, and live interpersonal sales work is a strong candidate for that lag. The rating holds at Low.
MKT 3981.d: Internships provide practical, hands-on experience in a professional field related to professional selling. The internship must be based on work that is new to the student and supervised by a sales professional. Internship placements must be approved through the internship credit approval process. Once enrolled, internship coursework is supervised by a faculty member. Students will complete academic work that encourages reflection regarding the approved learning objectives for the internship. Internship requirements vary by department. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

r: ProSales Team has students compete in live, in-person sales competitions hosted by universities and organizations, sharpening real-time selling skills and professionalism through travel to actual events and head-to-head performance evaluation — squarely Performing for or Working Directly with the Public and Selling or Influencing Others. This is the most embodied course in this batch: physical presence, live audience judging, real-time improvisation under competitive pressure, and travel logistics are not tasks a model performs, they are what the course is built around. Task-exposure research's finding that manual and in-person work sits at the low end of exposure applies with unusual directness here. No accreditation or gen-ed mandate is needed to explain the Low rating; the binding constraint is embodiment itself, and it is decisive regardless of how capable AI sales-support tools become elsewhere in the discipline.

Nothing about the physical-presence, live-competition structure of ProSales Team changes by 2031 in a way that shifts the rating. AI tools may help students draft pitch scripts or rehearse objection-handling before an event, but the graded, instrumental activity itself — standing in front of judges and prospects, adapting a pitch in real time, projecting professionalism under pressure — remains a psychomotor and interpersonal performance task outside language-model competence. The capability-trend literature describing fast general improvement in AI task-time horizons is about digital, decomposable tasks; live competitive selling is neither decomposable nor digital in this way. Diffusion of AI into sales-support workflows does not touch the competition format itself. The course holds at Low, with the embodiment dampener applying at full strength again, because the applied task the course trains for cannot be relocated into an AI-mediated channel without ceasing to be what it teaches.

Even at a ten-year horizon, live competitive sales performance — presence, real-time adaptation, judged interpersonal delivery — is a strong candidate to remain outside AI's competence in the way the embodiment factor anticipates, though the underlying task-automatability estimate does drift upward slightly to reflect uncertainty about how sales roles broadly evolve. The deterministic rule applies the dampener at this horizon too, holding the course at Low rather than letting the rising base rating through unchecked. This is a hedge: the METR/Epoch capability trend implies fast general progress, and it is conceivable AI-mediated remote selling formats grow enough to change what 'competitive selling' even means institutionally, but a physical, in-person competition format built on live audience judgment is a poor match for that shift. The rating reflects the structural, not merely technical, nature of the protection.
MKT 4020.d: This course is designed for students interested in competing in sales events hosted by universities and organizations. Content will focus on sharpening selling skills and professionalism during business trips and events. Students are expected to compete in at least one event and prepare team members for other events. Events vary by semester and may require travel (costs such as flight/ground transportation and hotel accommodations are covered by the Center for Professional Selling).

r: Brand Management has students assess brand equity, evaluate how marketing activities affect brand power, and build strategic action plans — Analyzing Data or Information and Developing Objectives and Strategies work. Brand audits, competitive positioning research, and even first-draft brand guideline documents are analytical, writing-heavy deliverables of exactly the kind observed-usage data shows AI already used for extensively, and GDPval-style evaluation of real occupational deliverables found current models approaching, though still below, human-expert parity on this class of work product. What is not yet reliably automated is the strategic judgment call — which brand-equity signal should actually drive an action plan for a specific company — that remains the course's real teaching target. With no gen-ed or accreditation designation in play, the Medium rating reflects that the supporting analysis is substantially exposed while the strategic decision layer still lags meaningfully behind it.

By 2031, the brand-analysis workflow this course teaches — competitive audits, equity tracking, guideline drafting, campaign impact assessment — is likely within reach of AI systems performing close to or above the GDPval benchmark's current near-parity mark on real deliverables, given the capability trend's pace of improvement. Task-exposure research's classification of writing as strongly positively associated with exposure supports this directly, since brand strategy documents are fundamentally written analytical artifacts. No embodiment, licensure, or foundational-course role protects Brand Management at this horizon, so the deterministic rule allows the rating to rise to High alongside the F1 increase. The residual — the final strategic call in a genuinely novel brand situation — is real, but it is a narrower slice of course content than the audit-and-plan work that dominates the syllabus.

A ten-year projection extends the same trajectory: if the capability trend toward longer AI task-time horizons continues at anything close to its recent pace, most of the brand-analysis and strategic-planning workflow this course covers becomes plausible for AI to execute with limited human input, and nothing in the factor structure — no gen-ed lock, no licensure gate, no foundational role feeding required courses — caps that rise. This is a hedge, not a certainty: brand strategy in genuinely novel competitive situations is a plausible edge case where the jagged-frontier literature's warning about AI users being less accurate outside a model's true competence could apply, and human brand leadership judgment may retain more residue than the deterministic rule captures. Still, the combination of high writing and analysis exposure with no institutional protection points to High.
MKT 4110.d: This course will cover brand management in-depth, demonstrate how marketing activities impact the power of an organization's brand, and examine the strategic importance of effectively managing a brand. Students will develop an ability to assess brands and implement action plans based on a strategic marketing orientation.

r: Content Marketing teaches students to plan and execute online content — blog posts, social media copy, editorial calendars — tied to an integrated marketing communication strategy, mapping to Interacting With Computers and Documenting/Recording Information. This is the most exposed course in the batch: content creation is a fully digital, writing-centric task, and task-exposure research finds writing strongly positively associated with automation exposure, while observed-usage data shows exactly this kind of office and writing work is already among the most common AI use cases today. Professional-writing productivity research reports large time reductions alongside quality gains on comparable drafting tasks, meaning much of the execution layer this course teaches is already competently AI-assisted. No embodiment, licensure, or gen-ed designation offers any protection here. The High rating at 24 months reflects that the instrumental case for manually producing this content is already substantially eroded.

By 2031, content marketing execution — draft generation, SEO optimization, content-calendar management, channel-specific adaptation — is likely performed competently by AI with only editorial oversight, extending the trajectory already visible in current usage data. The capability trend toward longer AI task-time horizons suggests multi-step content campaigns, not just individual posts, become manageable with minimal human drafting, and the strategic framing layer the course also teaches, such as audience definition and customer-lifecycle alignment, is itself expressible as a prompt and reviewable output rather than manual work. No institutional lock exists to slow this diffusion within the marketing discipline more broadly. The course remains High, with the residual human role concentrated narrowly in brand-voice calibration and final editorial approval rather than in the actual content production work itself.

At ten years, content marketing as this course teaches it — planning and producing content across the customer lifecycle to support brand and revenue goals — is a strong candidate for near-complete AI execution, consistent with both the writing-exposure finding in task-exposure research and the capability trend's implied trajectory. The primary hedge is that content strategy tied to brand identity and audience trust may retain a thin layer of human judgment even as production fully automates, and macro-level diffusion evidence suggests adoption, even where capability exists, may lag in smaller organizations for structural reasons. Neither qualification is strong enough to lower the rating given the deterministic rule and the complete absence of embodiment or institutional protection; the course stays High across all three horizons.
MKT 4200.d: Content marketing is a strategic approach to creating online content that furthers an organization's brand and ties into a broader integrated marketing communication strategy. It focuses on the creation of content that is useful for a clearly defined target audience throughout the customer life cycle and ultimately drives the organization's profitability. This course provides a framework for students to navigate the fast changing environment of the web and social media under the lens of content creation. Students will develop the skills needed to develop and execute a successful content marketing plan.

r: Advanced Selling has students integrate relationship selling, major-account selling, team selling, and live negotiation across complex B2B situations with multiple decision-makers, mapping to Resolving Conflicts and Negotiating with Others and Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships. Negotiating a multi-stakeholder deal in real time is both embodied — presence, tone, timing — and high-stakes: a misjudged concession or a misread signal from a buying committee carries real financial cost, so any AI assistance still needs a human who holds this specific relational and strategic knowledge to catch errors, consistent with the jagged-frontier finding that AI users are measurably less accurate outside a system's true competence. Proposal writing is a more exposed sub-task, but it is a minor share of what the course actually assesses. With no gen-ed or accreditation lock needed, embodiment and verification burden alone hold the course at Low.

AI negotiation-preparation and proposal-drafting tools are likely to mature by 2031, and observed-usage data already shows heavy adoption in office and writing tasks that touch parts of this course's proposal-writing component. But the graded, instrumental core of Advanced Selling — reading a room of multiple decision-makers, adapting a negotiation stance live, closing complex B2B deals — remains real-time interpersonal work under high verification burden, since a botched high-value negotiation is costly and non-obvious to catch after the fact. Both protective factors, embodiment and verification burden, persist unchanged at this horizon, so the dampener continues to apply even as the underlying task-automatability estimate rises modestly. The rating holds at Low; this reflects structural protection more than an assumption that AI capability in negotiation support stalls entirely.

Ten years out, AI-mediated negotiation support could plausibly extend further into deal preparation, scenario modeling, and even real-time coaching during a live negotiation, nudging the underlying automatability factor upward. But the deterministic rule applies the embodiment and verification-burden dampener at every horizon where the graded task remains live, multi-party, in-person or synchronous negotiation with real financial stakes, and that structural feature is not obviously removed by general capability gains the way a routine drafting task would be. This is a hedge, not a confident prediction: the capability trend literature shows fast improvement generally, and complex negotiation is exactly the kind of ambiguous, high-stakes task the jagged-frontier research flags as prone to AI overconfidence and human miscalibration. The rating stays at Low, reflecting that structural protection rather than a claim that AI will never assist here.
MKT 4250.d: Students sharpen the skills developed in sales classes to focus on relationship selling and integrate value-added selling, major account selling, team selling, negotiating, proposal writing, and business-to-business selling. Complex selling situations that involve multiple decision makers will be evaluated.

r: MKT 4300 builds skill in constructing social media marketing strategies, auditing a brand's positioning across platforms, and tracking campaign effectiveness within the course's zones-of-social-media framework. These tasks map to interacting-with-computers and communicating-with-persons-outside-the-organization activities, both squarely digital and inside the highest-exposure categories task-exposure research assigns to writers, marketers, and content producers. Observed-usage data already shows writing-adjacent and business-communication tasks among the leading categories of AI use, and generative tools routinely draft captions, content calendars, and basic performance summaries. At 24 months, though, brand-positioning judgment and platform-specific audience reading still require a trained marketer, and diffusion into day-to-day agency and in-house workflows remains partial and uneven. No general-studies designation or meaningful accreditation constraint binds this elective. The rating is Medium: execution-level content tasks are already substantially automatable, while the strategic-analysis core the course teaches has not yet been fully displaced.

By 2031, AI systems will competently perform the great majority of social media execution this course teaches: drafting and scheduling content, running sentiment and competitive audits, and generating effectiveness dashboards across platforms. Task-exposure research and observed-usage data both place this kind of content generation among the most automatable knowledge-work categories, and productivity studies on professional writing show large quality and speed gains from AI assistance that transfer directly to social copy and campaign materials. No embodiment, licensure, or foundational-scaffolding constraint protects the course, and the weak accreditation lock does not cap the rating. The residual is higher-order brand judgment and platform strategy, a real but shrinking share of the course's applied content. The rating rises to High: AI performs most of the instrumental work with limited human input, though the five-year projection carries real uncertainty about how quickly small-business and agency workflows actually adopt these tools at scale.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing nearly all routine social media execution and much of the audience and competitive analysis this course covers, leaving human marketers concentrated in brand strategy, platform-relationship management, and judgment calls AI handles less reliably. The instrumental case for a course built around building and auditing social strategy is substantially eroded under this trajectory, consistent with the capability trend of rapidly lengthening AI task horizons. The rating holds High, hedged by genuine ten-year uncertainty: adoption could lag capability, as diffusion data already show for 2025, and platform-specific strategic judgment could retain more value than a pure capability read implies. No institutional or foundational factor caps the rating at this horizon, so the projection tracks the underlying automatability trend rather than any structural protection.
MKT 4300.d: This course covers advertising, marketing, and communication strategies in the new media landscape where traditional media (e.g. television, print) and the online social media (e.g. Web 2.0, online social networks, usergenerated content, blogs, forums) co-exist. The primary focus of this course will be on understanding social media, how to build social media marketing strategies, and how to track their effectiveness. Students taking Social Media Marketing will learn the applications of social media to the fulfillment of marketing objectives, particularly those related to the promotion function of the marketing mix. In particular, students will be able to analyze the social context in which a brand operates and audit a brand's social media positioning, as well as develop strategies for marketing using the zones of social media.

r: MKT 4410 teaches students to leverage AI and machine-learning concepts for marketing decisions across content creation, advertising, product development, e-commerce, and sales, while critically examining the ethical, regulatory, and strategic risks of AI-driven marketing. The underlying execution tasks — generating content, running campaigns — sit in the highest-exposure categories task-exposure research identifies, but the course's actual center of gravity is evaluating and directing AI output, not producing it. That is a verification-heavy competency: the jagged-frontier finding that AI users outside the model's reliable range are measurably less accurate, with miscalibrated trust, is precisely the failure mode this course trains students to catch. At 24 months the rating is Low: near-term diffusion is limited and the course exists to build the oversight judgment that AI-driven marketing programs still require rather than to teach tasks AI already fully performs.

By 2031, AI will generate the large majority of the content, campaign structures, and product and e-commerce recommendations this course surveys, and observed-usage data already shows the automation share of enterprise AI use running well above augmentation. That raises exposure, but the course's ethical, regulatory, and strategic-evaluation content is the part of marketing work least substitutable by the systems it studies — judging bias, compliance, and brand risk in AI-generated output is a verification task, not an execution one, and the jagged-frontier evidence argues this judgment grows more valuable as reliance on AI output deepens. The dampening effect of that low verification burden keeps the rating from tracking pure content-generation exposure. The rating rises to Medium: execution automates substantially, but the course's core instructional content — teaching students to direct, audit, and govern AI marketing systems — remains instrumentally necessary.

A decade out, AI marketing execution will be pervasive and highly capable, and the central case has most content, targeting, and optimization work performed with minimal human drafting. Even so, this course's distinctive purpose — training students to evaluate AI outputs against ethical, regulatory, and strategic standards, and to make marketing decisions informed by that scrutiny — addresses exactly the oversight gap that persists when execution is heavily automated but accountability is not. The rating holds Medium, not High, because the verification-and-governance competence the course teaches is not itself displaced by better generation models; if anything, more capable and more widely deployed AI raises the stakes of that judgment. The ten-year projection carries real uncertainty about how marketing governance norms and regulation evolve, but the course's oversight function is unlikely to become instrumentally unnecessary.
MKT 4410.d: AI in Marketing: Creativity and Innovation explores the intersection of innovation and artificial intelligence (AI) in modern marketing. The course begins with the importance of creativity in marketing, followed by key theories of technological disruption and innovation. Students are introduced to AI and machine learning concepts and how they can be leveraged to make marketing decisions. Emphasis is placed on real-world applications including AI-powered content creation, social media, advertising, product development, e-commerce, and sales. The course also critically examines ethical, regulatory, and strategic challenges, preparing students to lead in the evolving landscape of AI-driven marketing.

r: MKT 4520 is the credit-earning arm of a student-run agency: teams execute real marketing deliverables for actual clients while learning to manage projects and client relationships, work effectively within a team, and develop professional judgment. The graded competence is not any single marketing artifact but the embodied, in-person practice of client management, team coordination, and professional conduct — activities task-exposure research places in low-exposure, high-presence categories distinct from the content-generation tasks that dominate marketing's overall exposure profile. Some deliverables (copy, analytics) are individually automatable, but the course's instrumental purpose is the supervised, real-world practice of running client relationships and teams, which AI does not perform on the student's behalf. At 24 months the rating is Low: embodiment and the interpersonal core of agency work protect the course even as component tasks are individually exposed.

By 2031, AI tools will handle more of the individual deliverables agency teams produce — draft copy, analytics, campaign reports — meaningfully augmenting student teams' output. But the course's actual instrumental content is professional practice itself: managing a live client relationship, coordinating a team under real deadlines, and developing the judgment and professionalism that only accrue through doing the work in a real agency context. That is an embodied, interpersonal competence that task-exposure research and productivity studies do not treat as automatable, since the value lies in the student's lived experience rather than the deliverable alone. No general-studies mandate protects the course, but embodiment does the protective work instead. The rating stays Low: component tasks automate, but the supervised professional-practice core the course exists to build is not something AI substitutes for the student.

Over a decade, AI will likely produce most of the routine marketing deliverables student teams currently execute by hand, shifting the agency's work further toward client strategy, relationship management, and oversight of AI-assisted production. Even so, the central instrumental purpose of MKT 4520 — giving students supervised, embodied practice managing real client relationships, coordinating teams, and building professional judgment — is not a task AI performs for the learner; it is defined by the student doing the work themselves. The rating holds Low under the central case, with real uncertainty about how much of the deliverable-production side of agency work automates around this still-human practicum core. The honest caveat is that the mix of tasks students perform will shift markedly, even as the course's rationale for existing — supervised professional practice — remains intact.
MKT 4520.d: This course is the credit-earning arm of a student-run marketing agency housed in the Department of Marketing. The agency provides students with real world, hands-on professional marketing experience that enables students to work in teams more closely resembling those in agencies and marketing departments than they find in classrooms. Students have opportunities to apply business and marketing knowledge to a broad range of marketing- related projects by actually executing marketing deliverables within working teams. Through the projects as well as in-class training, students learn to manage projects and client relationships; improve professionalism; identify measures of success; effectively work with a team; and develop personal learning goals.

r: MKT 4540 has students execute a real digital marketing campaign for an actual client, covering customer analysis, content strategy, and campaign planning, implementation, measurement, and evaluation, with platform-certification outcomes attached. These tasks — audience segmentation, content production, bid and channel optimization, performance measurement — map closely to interacting-with-computers and analyzing-data-or-information activities, and digital advertising platforms already automate much of the bidding and targeting work the course teaches students to run. Observed-usage data shows business-and-analytics tasks as a growing share of AI use, and controlled studies of AI-assisted technical work show large speed gains transferable to campaign execution and reporting. At 24 months the rating is Medium: platform tools already automate substantial execution, but the course's applied, client-facing implementation work and certification requirements still call for a trained practitioner running the process end to end.

By 2031, AI-driven campaign platforms will plausibly manage the bulk of targeting, bidding, content generation, and performance optimization this course trains students to execute manually, and observed-usage data already shows automation dominating augmentation in enterprise AI use for exactly this kind of operational marketing work. The client-facing implementation model — plan, execute, measure, evaluate — is the applied task the course's knowledge serves, and each stage is individually a high-exposure activity under task-exposure research. No embodiment, licensure, or foundational-scaffolding factor caps the erosion, and the weak business-college accreditation lock does not bind. The rating rises to High: AI performs most of the digital-execution work competently with limited human direction, leaving customer-analysis judgment and client relationship management as the narrower residual that keeps some human role intact.

A decade out, the central case has AI managing nearly all routine digital-campaign execution — targeting, content generation, bid optimization, and reporting — with human marketers concentrated in client strategy and campaign oversight rather than hands-on implementation. The instrumental case for a course centered on executing and measuring a digital campaign is substantially eroded under this trajectory, tracking the capability trend of rapidly expanding AI task horizons in exactly the digital, measurable, feedback-rich domain this course occupies. The rating holds High, hedged by genuine ten-year uncertainty about how quickly platform automation actually diffuses into small-business and agency practice, as current diffusion data already show real lags behind raw capability. No institutional or foundational factor caps the rating, so the projection follows the underlying automatability of digital execution rather than any structural protection.
MKT 4540.d: In this course, students apply advanced, hands-on digital marketing skills in the context of overall business and marketing strategy. The course includes customer analysis, content strategy, and digital marketing planning, implementation, measurement, and evaluation. The course qualifies students for certifications in current, relevant digital marketing platforms. Students gain experience by working with a team to develop and execute a digital marketing campaign for a real-world client.

r: MKT 4560 has students use quantitative and qualitative data to analyze trends, competitors, and customers, then build branding, positioning, and long-term customer-relationship strategies. Trend and competitor analysis and quantitative synthesis map to analyzing-data-or-information activities that are already substantially AI-assisted, and observed-usage data shows analytical and business-communication tasks among the leading AI-use categories. But the course's second half — establishing strategic positioning and cultivating durable customer relationships — carries a real interpersonal and judgment component that resists full automation, and real-deliverable benchmarks still show AI trailing human experts on complex, judgment-laden strategic work. At 24 months the rating is Medium: quantitative analysis is heavily augmented already, while the strategic-synthesis and relationship-building core the course builds toward has not yet been meaningfully displaced, and diffusion into strategic planning workflows remains partial.

By 2031, AI will competently perform most of the analytical work this course teaches — trend analysis, competitive benchmarking, customer-data synthesis — and will draft credible strategic and positioning recommendations directly from that analysis. Task-exposure research consistently ranks this kind of quantitative-analytical and writing-adjacent work among the most automatable categories, and no licensure, embodiment, or foundational-scaffolding factor caps the course's exposure; the business college's accreditation body sets no course-specific mandate. The residual is higher-order strategic judgment and the relationship-building dimension of long-term customer strategy, real but a shrinking share of the course's applied content as AI-generated strategic recommendations improve. The rating rises to High: the applied analytical and planning work is performed competently by AI with limited human input, even as strategic judgment and client relationships remain a genuine, if narrowing, human residual.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing nearly all quantitative market analysis and generating strategic recommendations of real quality, per the capability trend of fast-doubling task horizons, leaving human marketers concentrated in relationship stewardship and contested strategic judgment. The instrumental case for a course centered on analysis-driven strategy formation is substantially eroded under this trajectory. The rating holds High, hedged by real ten-year uncertainty: GDPval-style benchmarks show AI still trailing human experts on complex real-world deliverables even as it approaches parity, and it is plausible that senior strategic judgment and customer-relationship work retain more human value than a pure capability read implies. No institutional or foundational factor caps the rating, so the projection tracks the underlying analytical-automatability trend rather than structural protection.
MKT 4560.d: Students in this course engage in an in-depth examination of marketing analysis techniques and the development of strategic marketing plans. Students learn how to use quantitative and qualitative data to make informed marketing decisions and create effective strategies that align with business objectives. Key topics include analysis of trends, competitors, and customers; establishing branding and strategic positioning; and developing long-term customer relationships. Mathematical Sciences
